title: The bounded payer writes every payment record from literals (Orchard -> Orchard, Shielded, FullPrivacy) and never applies the recipient-policy guard, so a payment whose transaction crosses a shielded pool boundary (a Sapling receiver) would be recorded and scored as a same-pool, fully-shielded, FullPrivacy payment
description: payer::run pays each invoice it admitted through ops::propose_shielded_payment / ops::build_sign_broadcast and then records the payment at payer.rs:339-362, where pool_in: Pool::Orchard (349), pool_out: Pool::Orchard (350), kind: PaymentKind::Shielded (351) and policy: Some("FullPrivacy") (352) are constants: none is derived from the proposal or the transaction, and payer.rs never reads the proposal back (0 occurrences of proposal.steps / payment_pools / any transaction decryption, against ops.rs:1076-1126 where `pay` decrypts the mined transaction). observation/src/lib.rs:28-30 defines PaymentKind::Shielded as "shielded source and shielded destination, same pool" and 56-60 defines pool_out as the payment's destination pool and `policy` as "the privacy policy argument the flow passed to its wallet layer, verbatim" - the payer passes no such argument. This path also never calls ops::required_policy_for_recipient + ops::check_policy (payer.rs: 0 call sites; every other payment path does: ops.rs:563-566, 777, 1019-1020; flow.rs:633-634, 826-827), and ops::propose_shielded_payments (payer.rs:306-307 -> ops.rs:900-961) applies SpendPolicy::shielded_pools([Orchard]) to input sources only (zcash_client_backend 0.24.0 input_selection.rs:476-489, 966-968, 999-1003). The recipient comes from the merchant's invoice file, deserialized directly (payer.rs:495-519, no ZIP-321 cross-check unlike flow.rs:1740-1768), and decide only string-compares it against the grant allowlist (payer.rs:100); an empty or absent allowlist admits every receiver (printed at payer.rs:222-224). A merchant-supplied invoice naming a Sapling receiver therefore reaches the wallet layer: verifier-2 reproduced this in the offline sandbox - the payer's own intake took the dev account's bare zregtestsapling1 receiver and a Sapling-only UA to "Must scan blocks first" (fundless stub wallet, identical to the Orchard control), while required_policy_for_recipient + check_policy refuse those same recipients under FullPrivacy with "would reveal the amount (Orchard -> Sapling pool crossing)" (ops.rs:243-246). The record then decides every verdict derived from it: policy-downgrade (Severity::Disqualifying) computes its explicit signal from Payment.policy (76-89; "FullPrivacy" matches no downgrade fragment) and its implicit signal from pool_in (shielded) plus pool_out in {Transparent, CrossPool} (92-101), so the payer's constant record makes it PASS - reproduced with zanary_properties::evaluate() in the sandbox, where the fixtures' honest cross-pool record (fixtures.rs:243-246) FAILs as a positive control. Nothing re-derives a pool leg afterwards: report/src/verify.rs re-checks tx height / receiver / memo / pool totals as report evidence and the report crate never mentions pool_in/pool_out, and no property compares run.payments against the ledger or the chain. Calibration: the flow runner writes the same Orchard/Orchard/Shielded constants (flow.rs:687-690, 984-987) but records the real policy token and does gate recipients, and the property's implicit signal does not cover pool_out Sapling at all - the record lie is what turns an undetected crossing into a recorded, scored "fully private" payment.
claimed_root_cause: Two coupled defects on the payer's pay path: (1) the record fields the leak properties read are literals - pool_in/pool_out/kind/policy at payer.rs:349-352 are never derived from the proposal's payment pools or from the built transaction, so they describe what the payer assumed rather than what it built; (2) the payer is the only payment path in the workspace that does not call ops::required_policy_for_recipient + ops::check_policy before proposing (0 call sites in payer.rs against ops.rs:563-566/777/1019-1020 and flow.rs:633-634/826-827), so a merchant-supplied recipient that makes the payment reveal more than FullPrivacy (a Sapling receiver, which the target's own intake accepts and hands to the wallet layer) is paid instead of refused, and is then recorded as Orchard -> Orchard Shielded FullPrivacy.

trace.scope: payer::run - the payment loop over the invoices decide allowed
trace.description: The merchant-supplied receiver (deserialized straight from the invoice JSON at payer.rs:495-519, with no ZIP-321 cross-check unlike flow.rs:1740-1768) is decoded into the address the payment will be made to; there is no recipient-kind or privacy-policy gate anywhere on this path (payer.rs has 0 occurrences of check_policy / required_policy_for_recipient).

The recipient becomes a ZIP-321 payment handed to propose_transfer with SpendPolicy::shielded_pools([Orchard]) (inputs only; 929) and an Orchard change strategy (931-936), so nothing constrains the recipient's own pool. Reproduced: a bare Sapling receiver and a Sapling-only UA pass this intake and reach the wallet layer ("Must scan blocks first" in a fundless stub wallet), while required_policy_for_recipient + check_policy refuse the same recipients under FullPrivacy (ops.rs:243-246).

Whatever the proposal built is proved, signed, read back from the wallet (396-402) and sent to the indexer (407-415) without any comparison against the invoice the payer decided about and without inspecting the transaction's pools.

trace.scope: payer::run - the Payment record written for the payment just broadcast
trace.description: pool_in, pool_out, kind and policy are written as constants (349-352: Orchard / Orchard / Shielded / FullPrivacy), so the run's evidence - and the findings, report and index built from it - assert a same-pool, fully-shielded, FullPrivacy payment regardless of the transaction's real shape; policy-downgrade (Disqualifying) reads exactly these fields and passes (reproduced).

evidence.description: the four fields policy-downgrade reads are literals: pool_in: Pool::Orchard (349), pool_out: Pool::Orchard (350), kind: PaymentKind::Shielded (351), policy: Some("FullPrivacy") (352); payer.rs reads nothing back (0 occurrences of proposal.steps / payment_pools / decrypt - verifier-2's sandbox count over the compiled file)

required_policy_for_recipient maps a Sapling receiver (or a UA with a Sapling receiver and no Orchard receiver, 250-254) to AllowRevealedAmounts because the payment would reveal "the amount (Orchard -> Sapling pool crossing)" (243-246)

the CLI pay path calls check_policy before proposing (1019-1020); ops.rs:563-566 (anchor), ops.rs:777 (shield) and flow.rs:633-634 / 826-827 do the same; payer.rs has no equivalent (0 occurrences, verifier-2 sandbox count)

the implicit-downgrade signal is computed from Payment.pool_in/pool_out alone (92-101; reveal requires pool_out Transparent|CrossPool) and the explicit one from Payment.policy (76-89; "FullPrivacy" matches no fragment), so the constant record decides the verdict - reproduced: zanary_properties::evaluate() returns PASS for the payer's record and FAIL for the fixtures' honest cross-pool control
policy-downgrade is Severity::Disqualifying (54-56), so the false PASS is published as a clean verdict for a run whose payment actually crossed a shielded pool boundary

PaymentKind::Shielded is defined as "shielded source and shielded destination, same pool" (28-30); pool_out is the payment's destination pool and `policy` the "privacy policy argument the flow passed to its wallet layer, verbatim" (56-60) - recording Orchard/Shielded/FullPrivacy for a Sapling-output payment is false by the model's own definitions, and the payer passed no such argument

the fixture that models a cross-pool payment records the real destination pool (pool_in Orchard, pool_out Transparent, kind CrossPool, policy AllowRevealedAmounts; 243-246) and drives the property's failing path - used here as the positive control that the property bites when the record is honest
the harness chain activates Sapling at height 1 (84-96) while NU6.1/6.2/6.3 (Ironwood) stay unactivated, so a Sapling output is the shielded cross-pool delivery this build can produce

dependency source (version pinned by Cargo.toml:20, vendored read-only): GreedyInputSelector::propose_transaction delivers an Address::Sapling recipient through a Sapling output with payment_pools[idx] = SAPLING (966-968; a Sapling-only UA at 999-1003), and SpendPolicy::shielded_pools constrains input sources only (476-489) - so the transaction built for a Sapling-receiver invoice carries the Sapling leg the record denies (source-corroborated; not executed - see blockers)

calibration: the flow runner writes the same Orchard/Orchard/Shielded constants (687-690, 984-987) but records the real policy token (Some(policy.name())) and calls the guard at 633-634 / 826-827 - the template pattern is shared, while the missing guard is specific to the payer

`zanary-report verify` re-derives tx height / receiver / memo / pool-total evidence from the chain, and the report crate never mentions pool_in/pool_out (0 occurrences): nothing re-derives or cross-checks the recorded pool legs
the decision only string-compares the receiver against the grant allowlist; an empty or absent allowlist admits every receiver and is printed as such at 222-224

blockers: The decisive step - that the proposal/transaction built for a Sapling-receiver invoice carries a Sapling output - could not be executed in the approved sandbox: it needs a wallet holding a spendable Orchard note, and no offline route exists (zcash_client_backend's test-wallet framework needs the test-dependencies feature set -> proptest/ambassador/assert_matches, none of which are in the read-only registry cache - verifier-2 confirmed the cache holds only incrementalmerkletree/rand_chacha/tempfile of that set - and --network=none permits no fetch). The leg is Sapling by source (input_selection.rs:966-968, 999-1003); execution is what is missing.

The end of the path - the broadcast, the mined transaction's shape, and the report/index published from the run - needs the regtest rig (its containers and host ports 18232/18233/9067/9068), which is out of bounds.

Whether a Sapling-receiver invoice ever reaches a payer in practice is a deployment fact: every recorded run on this host and the CI demo issue Orchard-only invoices with a 3-receiver allowlist (data/grants/*.json, data/demo-payer/invoices/*.json, scripts/bounded-payer-demo.sh), while the payer's contract is any invoice directory and no observation of a Sapling-receiver invoice reaching a payer exists.

Without that framework, verifier-2 already re-established everything short of the proposal in /t (crates/probe/src/bin/verifier2_check.rs; output check-verify2.txt): payer.rs:349-352 are literals and payer.rs calls neither guard; the Sapling receiver reaches the wallet layer through the payer's own intake while required_policy_for_recipient + check_policy refuse it; zanary_properties::evaluate() gives the constant record policy-downgrade PASS (and the fixtures' honest cross-pool record FAIL).

Non-destructive control on the same invoice (refuses before proposing or broadcasting): `zanary-probe pay --invoice <the same file> --policy FullPrivacy` must refuse at ops.rs:1019-1020 with "would reveal the amount (Orchard -> Sapling pool crossing)".

title: Report CLI truncates untrusted report/run JSON fields by byte index and panics (exit 101) instead of returning a verdict
description: The zanary-report CLI deserializes a report/run file supplied by the claim's publisher and passes its flow_commit and report_hash into the display helpers short()/short_tail(), which truncate with byte indices. Any value whose truncation offset falls inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character aborts the process with a char-boundary panic, before or while the checks are printed. The verifier is documented as the stranger's check on a claim it does not trust ('Nothing here may depend on the reporter's honesty', crates/report/src/lib.rs:10; the fixtures README invites editing a report and re-running), and the tool's contract is exit 0 on pass, 1 on any mismatch, 2 on error; the trigger reaches the panic with no node, no indexer and no keys.
root_cause: short() (crates/report/src/main.rs:760-765) formats `&hash[..12]` (line 762) and short_tail() (main.rs:283-288) formats `&value[..8]`/`&value[value.len() - 8..]` (line 287); the matrix renderer (matrix.rs:109 and :148, and the CLI summary at main.rs:226) slices `&column.commit[..8.min(len)]`. The inputs are Report.flow_commit / Report.report_hash / FlowRun.flow_commit deserialized from caller-supplied JSON (crates/report/src/lib.rs:33-55, crates/observation/src/lib.rs:154-157) and never validated as ASCII or hex, so the slices are not on guaranteed char boundaries. The identical helper shape is duplicated in crates/report/src/verify.rs:849-855 (used at verify.rs:673, the report-hash-mismatch branch, which a hostile report_hash always takes because the recomputed value is a 64-char hex digest), and also at crates/report/src/index.rs:136-138 (applied to report.flow_commit/report_hash at index.rs:298/314/326) and crates/report/src/receipt.rs:188-190 (applied to attestation key strings at receipt.rs:145-153).
intended_behavior: Fields that stand in for hashes should be validated at intake (or the truncation made character-safe), and every command should end in its documented verdict: verify exits 0 when every check passes, 1 on any mismatch, 2 on error; matrix either renders or fails with a diagnostic. A report the verifier does not trust must be handled as data, never as something that can terminate the process.

The same untrusted report.report_hash reaches verify.rs's own copy of short() (verify.rs:851) exactly in the branch that exists to print the mismatch — the branch a hostile report_hash always takes, since the recomputed hash is 64 hex ASCII characters.

`&hash[..12]` panics with 'end byte index 12 is not a char boundary' when the field's byte 12 falls inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character: stdout stays empty, no check line and no verdict is produced, exit code 101 (observed panic location main.rs:762:29).

main() documents the exit contract: Ok(code) -> exit(code), Err -> exit(2); a panic bypasses it with exit 101 (controls: benign verify 1, missing file 2, benign build/matrix 0; hostile inputs 101).

No memory-safety, confidentiality or privilege effect observed in any run.

remediation.strategy: Make the display truncation character-safe and stop accepting non-hash text in hash fields. Either reject at intake (validate that flow_commit/report_hash are ASCII hex before anything else runs, exiting 2 with the existing error style) or truncate on character boundaries; add one regression case per command that feeds a multi-byte field and asserts the documented exit code. The same two-line helper shape is duplicated in the verify, index and receipt modules; the fix should replace every copy (main.rs, verify.rs, matrix.rs including the CLI summary at main.rs:226, index.rs, receipt.rs) so a later caller cannot reintroduce the byte slice.

likelihood.reason: The trigger is a few bytes in a JSON field the claimant fully controls and no layer validates them, but this rig's own pipeline always writes ASCII hex hashes, so it takes an adversarial or hand-authored claimant rather than ordinary operation.

impact.reason: Observable effect is safe process termination: the checking process aborts (exit 101) and produces no verdict, replacing the documented 0/1/2 contract; build additionally exits 101 after writing its artifact, so automation sees a failure with output on disk. No memory-safety, confidentiality or privilege effect was observed, and the failure is fail-closed for a verifier.

confidence.reason: Complete source trace from the parsed JSON field to the exact panicking expressions, re-derived line by line, then reproduced end-to-end in the approved sandbox: verify/build/matrix/verify-anchor all exit 101 with the predicted char-boundary panics at main.rs:762:29, verify.rs:851:29, main.rs:287:28 and matrix.rs:109:27, with a benign control for every command showing the documented behaviour.

title: verify-receipt aborts with a Rust panic (exit 101, no verdict) on a receipt whose hex fields or attestation key are not ASCII
description: `zanary-report verify-receipt` exists so a stranger can check a receipt somebody else supplied: main.rs:104-106 reads the path from argv and deserializes it into `zanary_observation::Receipt`, whose `signer`, `signature` and `attestation.{format,receipt_key,wallet_ak,signature}` fields are arbitrary UTF-8 `String`s (crates/observation/src/lib.rs:115-141), and receipt.rs then slices those strings by BYTE offset - `hex_decode` (receipt.rs:352-363, reached from receipt.rs:65,72,157,165) and the display helper `short` (receipt.rs:188-194, reached from main.rs:188-189 and receipt.rs:145-146,151-154). `hex_decode` only checks that the byte length is even before `u8::from_str_radix(&hex[i..i + 2], 16)`, and `short` only checks `hex.len() > 20` before `&hex[..8]` / `&hex[hex.len() - 8..]` on the same line; slicing a `&str` panics when the index falls inside a multi-byte character. A receipt whose `signer` is `a\u20ac` (4 bytes, even) aborts the verifier before any verdict line is printed; a receipt whose signed fields are perfectly valid and which carries an `attestation` object whose `receipt_key` is not ASCII passes `signature : VALID` and both `claim ok` lines and then panics inside `short()` on the no-`--fvk` branch (main.rs:184-190) - reachable because the attestation is not part of the signed bytes, as the crate's own test asserts (receipt.rs:487-504) and as this verifier re-established by attaching the attestation after signing and still seeing `signature : VALID`. The tool's contract is an exit code a caller or workflow reads (0 verified, 1 FAIL, 2 input error; main.rs:49-55, 135-137, 199-200); a panic is none of those, so for that artifact the caller gets no verdict at all. Both variants were independently reproduced by this verifier in the sandbox from fixtures generated by the target's own signing code (check-cli-repro.txt, check-unit-probe.txt).
root_cause: Byte-offset slicing of caller-controlled strings guarded only by a byte length: `hex_decode` slices `&hex[i..i + 2]` (receipt.rs:359) after `hex.len().is_multiple_of(2)` (receipt.rs:353) and `short` slices `&hex[..8]` and `&hex[hex.len() - 8..]` (receipt.rs:190) after `hex.len() > 20` (receipt.rs:189). Neither calls `is_char_boundary` nor rejects non-ASCII, so any multi-byte UTF-8 character straddling an index panics with "end byte index N is not a char boundary".
intended_behavior: Malformed receipt fields are reported, not fatal: the existing error paths return `hex string has an odd length`, `the signer key is N bytes, expected 32` and `the signer key is not a valid Orchard spend-authorizing key`, the CLI prints `signature : INVALID` / `claim : INVALID` and exits 1, and `--fvk` mismatches exit 1 (main.rs:120-138, 174-181; receipt.rs:352-363; docs/FLOW-RUNNER-NOTES.md:343-355 documents the same malformed-receipt rows as exit 1). Every parseable receipt file should produce a verdict with exit 0 (pass), 1 (FAIL) or 2 (input error, e.g. an undecodable UFVK) - never a process abort; the ASCII controls in this verification exit 0 on the same binaries.

title: verify-receipt certifies claim/body agreement for a receipt whose claims state different figures (substring containment)
description: `validate_claim` is documented as the machine-readable half of "a stranger can check it": receipt.rs:250-256 says the rules are the ones in schemas/zanary-receipt-v1.json and that "a claim that contradicts the body ... fails here rather than being printed as if it were fine", and receipt.rs:308-310 says "the words must state the figures". The implementation (receipt.rs:311-322) joins the claims into one string and tests `words.contains(&needle)` for the txid, the amount and the invoice id - pure substring containment - and never checks that the claims state nothing else. A claim that names a DIFFERENT invoice id and a DIFFERENT amount, with the body's values embedded as digit substrings, therefore passes: the executed receipt carries body invoice 4471 / 1234567 zatoshis and the claim "invoice 44710 was paid 12345678 zatoshis in transaction 44f2...337e", and `verify-receipt` prints both `claim ok` lines and exits 0 (independently re-executed by the verifier, including on a freshly signed fixture whose claim states invoice 91207 / 2500000 zatoshis for a body of 9120 / 250000). The claim text is the human-readable half of the artifact (it is inside the signed payload, receipt.rs:24-29; printed before any check runs, main.rs:110-111; rendered as claim="..." in the report-leak property's evidence, report_leak.rs:108-115), so a receipt can state a ten times larger payment for a different invoice while the tool that exists to check it certifies the two halves agree.
root_cause: The claim/body agreement test is `receipt.claims.join(" ").contains(&needle)` (receipt.rs:311-322, the test at 317). Containment is satisfied by any superstring, so the test accepts claims that state different figures than the body whenever the body's digits appear inside the claim's (larger) numbers, and it never requires the claims to state nothing else. The refusal the docs promise fires only when the body's figures are entirely absent (verified: a claim naming invoice 9121 for a body of 9120 is refused with "never state the invoice id (9120)"). The shipped schema's promise ("refuses a receipt whose claims contradict its body") is not implemented, and the schema's prose cannot express the missing rule.
intended_behavior: A receipt whose claims and body disagree is refused: validate_claim returns Err and the CLI prints `claim : INVALID - the claims never state the amount in zatoshis (999) that its body carries` and exits 1. That is the documented behaviour for the bundled disagreement fixture (docs/FLOW-RUNNER-NOTES.md:352; docs/FLOW-RUNNER-PLAN.md:127-131: "claims that state the body's figures ... claims-vs-body disagreement -> exit 1 with a precise message each").

title: Bounded payer follows symlinks and blocks forever on non-regular *.json entries in the merchant-supplied invoice directory
description: load_invoices (crates/probe/src/payer.rs:495-520) selects entries by the json extension alone (line 503) and reads each with std::fs::read_to_string (line 513). A symlinked *.json is followed and read from outside the supplied directory (verifier-reproduced: an invoice living outside --invoices was loaded, decided and queued), and a FIFO named *.json makes the process block in open() indefinitely (verifier-reproduced: the process was alive and sleeping with kernel wchan wait_for_partner after 5 s and 10 s, zero bytes of output, SIGKILL at ~10 s and exit 137) - there is no regular-file check, no O_NOFOLLOW and no timeout anywhere in intake. A party able to create one entry in the directory can therefore hang the payer before any authority evaluation (even a revoked grant never reaches its refusal) and can make the payer read and queue a file outside the directory it was given. Calibration: the report crate applies is_file() to its input paths (crates/report/src/main.rs:716) while the payer intake does not, and the repo's CI payer job bound (timeout-minutes: 60, .github/workflows/privacy-gate.yml:223) limits an unattended CI hang without preventing it.
root_cause: The entry type is never validated: the extension filter (payer.rs:503) is the only selection rule, and read_to_string (payer.rs:513) both follows symlinks and blocks in open() on FIFOs, with no read deadline.
intended_behavior: Only regular files inside the supplied directory should be read: reject symlinks and non-regular entries (symlink_metadata/file_type check, or an O_NOFOLLOW open) as ledger-able refusals, and put a deadline on intake reads so one blocking entry cannot hold the payer hostage.

title: Bounded payer ingests a merchant-supplied invoice directory into memory with no size or count cap, before and independent of grant authority
description: load_invoices (crates/probe/src/payer.rs:495-520) enumerates every *.json entry under the --invoices path, reads each file whole with std::fs::read_to_string (payer.rs:513) and parses it with serde_json::from_str (payer.rs:515), retaining every parsed Invoice in one Vec (payer.rs:517). There is no per-file size cap, no invoice-count cap and no memory budget anywhere in 495-520; the only accounting in the payer is decide()'s monetary budget over amount_zat (payer.rs:119-128). The whole intake runs before the first decide() call (payer.rs:201 vs 249-250) and is not conditional on the grant state computed at payer.rs:187-199, so it is performed even when the grant is revoked or the kill file exists: the kill switch limits payments, not intake work. Caused by: out of memory' and zero decision lines; 5000 tiny invoice files are all read, accepted (ALLOW) and queued in one run. Each allowed invoice is additionally cloned into to_pay (payer.rs:259) for the payment phase.
root_cause: The invoice directory is an untrusted merchant channel, but intake is unbounded and unconditional: read_dir collects an unlimited number of *.json entries (payer.rs:498-506), read_to_string reads each one whole with the file's own size hint deciding the allocation (payer.rs:513), every parsed Invoice is retained in one Vec (payer.rs:511-517) and each allowed one is cloned into the payment queue (payer.rs:259) - with no size cap, no count cap, no metadata size or regular-file check, and no consideration of the grant or kill-switch state (payer.rs:187-199) before the work.

title: Bounded payer queues an unbounded number of payments: the grant bounds the sum of amounts, not the count of heavy per-invoice work
description: run() appends every invoice decide() allows to to_pay with no cardinality cap (payer.rs:249-260) and then pays them one at a time (payer.rs:291-309). Each queued entry costs fixed heavy work: a proposal (ops.rs:884-891), an Orchard build/prove/sign and broadcast through the indexer (ops.rs:360-428), then 11 mined blocks plus a wallet resync (payer.rs:309 -> ops.rs:433-451; CONFIRM_BLOCKS = 11 at ops.rs:59). The grant bounds only each amount and the running sum of amount_zat (payer.rs:110-128), so zero-amount invoices never consume the 50,000,000-zat default budget (payer.rs:64-66) and one-zat invoices fit up to 50,000,000 payments, while the attacker's per-payment input is one small JSON file (~140 B). Independently reproduced from a fresh build of the pinned revision inside the sandbox: 5,000 zero-amount invoices were all read, decided ALLOW and queued in one run ('invoices : 5000', 5,000 ALLOW lines, ~1 s), and a 300-file one-zat run with budget 150 admitted exactly 150 (the sum-of-amounts budget was the only count-limiting check). The run then requires the harness node (payer.rs:275-276) and stops with 'Connection refused' in --network=none, so the payment work itself, its per-payment cost and the effect of N sequential payments on the shared regtest node are owner-rig observations this audit cannot make.

title: Composite action expands caller-supplied with: inputs into shell script text
description: action.yml is published as a composite action that third-party workflows run (`uses: memeshee/zanary@main` is the documented whole setup: action.yml:7, docs/CI.md:49). Its five inputs (flow, expect, anchor, ttl-days, out; action.yml:23-46) are free-form strings with no validation, and the action places their `${{ inputs.* }}` values in the script text of its `run:` steps -- the gate step (:95, :100, :103, :106, :116, :117), the always-run job summary step (:140) and the verdict step (:177-178) -- instead of receiving them through env: or argv. The runner substitutes those expressions into the script before bash parses it, so a value carrying shell syntax (a quote plus ;, $( ), backticks, #) is executed by the calling job's shell. The gate step also writes the value derived from inputs.out into GITHUB_OUTPUT as one raw, unescaped line (:107), so the value leaves the step as a step output and is re-interpolated into script text at :136 (job summary, `if: always()`) and :153 (rig diagnostics); the verdict step interpolates the step's exit_code output the same way (:175, numeric in this action's flow). Nothing in this repository triggers it: the documented consumer setup passes literal values (docs/CI.md:49-55, the flow literal at :51) and this repository's own gate passes static matrix entries defined in the same file (.github/workflows/privacy-gate.yml:87-93 from the matrix at :71-80). The defect is in the action as a library: it hands every consumer that templates one of the five inputs into `with:` a code-execution sink in that consumer's own job.
root_cause: The action treats caller-supplied input values as script fragments rather than data. `${{ inputs.* }}` values are placed in `run:` script text at eight sites (:95, :100, :103, :106, :116, :117, :140, :177-178, counting the two verdict lines as one site), and no value is passed through env: or argv anywhere in the file (action.yml has no env: block at all). title: verify-invoice panics on a txid containing a multi-byte UTF-8 character instead of rejecting it
description: flow::hex_decode checks only that the txid's byte length is even, then slices the string with `&hex[i..i + 2]`. Rust &str indices are byte offsets, so any input whose even UTF-8 byte length lets a 2-byte slice boundary land inside a multi-byte character aborts the process (exit 101, `end byte index N is not a char boundary`) instead of returning the normal `invalid hex at byte N` error (exit 1). verify-invoice decodes --txid before it opens a wallet or touches the chain, so the crash is reachable offline with a four-byte argument. The same workspace decodes hex safely in two other places (crates/report/src/node.rs:193-203 and crates/probe/src/bin/zanary-seed.rs:714-723 both step over `hex.as_bytes().chunks(2)` and map a bad chunk to an error), and the same function's other rejections are clean (odd length and non-hex input both exit 1), so the panicking shape is an outlier rather than a deliberate fail-loudly choice.
root_cause: flow::hex_decode (crates/probe/src/flow.rs:1778-1789) byte-indexes a &str — `u8::from_str_radix(&hex[i..i + 2], 16)` at flow.rs:1785 — after validating only that the byte length is even; a multi-byte UTF-8 character straddling a 2-byte slice boundary makes the slice panic.
intended_behavior: A --txid that is not hex is refused with `Error: decoding the txid ... invalid hex at byte N` and exit 1 (the odd-length case with `hex string has an odd length`), as every other bad-txid shape already is.

trace.description: `Some("verify-invoice") => flow::verify_invoice(rest).await` passes the caller's raw argv to the command
the --txid value is captured verbatim from argv (`txid_hex = Some(value(i, "--txid")?)`), with no character-level validation
`hex_decode(&txid_hex)` runs before `core::bootstrap_with(WalletProfile::merchant(...))` at flow.rs:1699-1700, so no wallet, node or indexer is involved

`&hex[i..i + 2]` slices at byte offsets; an offset inside a multi-byte character panics (verifier-11 repro: --txid "aéb" (bytes 61 c3 a9 62) -> exit 101, `panicked at crates/probe/src/flow.rs:1785:36: end byte index 2 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 1..3 of string)`)

sibling control: the report crate's hex_decode iterates `hex.as_bytes().chunks(2)` and converts each chunk with std::str::from_utf8, returning an error instead of panicking
sibling control: zanary-seed's hex_decode_into (lines 714-723) iterates `hex.as_bytes().chunks(2)` and returns an error via std::str::from_utf8

title: The grant's budget bounds invoice principal, not the cost of paying: per-payment fees and the invoice count sit outside the authority
description: docs/BOUNDED-PAYER.md defines budget as "the most the run may spend in total" (line 28), and observation::PayerRun::spent_zat() labels its sum "Zatoshis actually spent under this grant" (observation/src/lib.rs:233-234). decide()'s budget rule (payer.rs:119-128) adds only invoice amounts, and the payer-policy property re-derives exactly the same number (payer_policy.rs:77-90), while the payer's own funding model budgets one ZIP-317 fee per payment at 10_000 zat (payer.rs:528-530; the runner's fee budget agrees, flow.rs:1165-1177) — a cost the grant never counts. With no minimum invoice amount (Invoice.amount_zat is a bare u64, flow.rs:1544) and no cap on how many invoices a run may load, decide and pay (load_invoices, payer.rs:495-520), a merchant can make the run's real spend dwarf the granted budget: 1-zat invoices fill a 1,000-zat budget with 1,000 payments and ~10,000,000 zat of fees, each payment also costing 11 mined blocks and a wallet sync (payer.rs:309, ops.rs:59). The ledger and payer-policy report 1,000 of 1,000 zat spent. Re-verified by execution: the real decide() admits the full thousand and the real payer-policy property passes the resulting ledger. Calibration: the flow runner funds fees the same way but holds no grant, so only the payer's authority claim is contradicted.
root_cause: The budget and per-payment cap are denominated in invoice principal only: neither decide()'s budget rule (payer.rs:119-128) nor the payer-policy re-derivation (payer_policy.rs:77-90) counts the per-payment fee the payer's own funding model budgets (payer.rs:530), and the grant schema has no cap on the number of payments (or a minimum amount) even though each payment carries a fixed-cost floor for the operator (one ZIP-317 fee, one 11-block mining round, one wallet sync).
intended_behavior: The grant's budget is the operator's bound on what the run spends ("the most the run may spend in total", docs/BOUNDED-PAYER.md:28; ledger/property summary "N of M zat spent"): a run at its budget must not be able to cost the operator an unbounded multiple of it.

only invoice principal is accumulated (spent_zat.saturating_add(invoice.amount_zat), 119; refuse only when after > budget_zat, 120): a 1-zat invoice is always affordable until the nominal budget is exhausted

shortfall(&payer, &to_pay) (523-533) budgets sum(amounts) + 10_000 zat per payment (530) and flow::top_up_for_target (286; flow.rs:1202) mines/shields that headroom from outside the grant — the fee spend is real to the operator but invisible to the authority

title: Bounded payer enforces grant expiry as a text comparison, so an expiry instant written with a UTC offset (or an unparsable value) still pays
description: decide() refuses an invoice only when the ASCII comparison `now >= grant.expires_at` holds (crates/probe/src/payer.rs:91). Both sides are unvalidated strings: `now` comes from the workspace clock (RFC3339 Z, fractional seconds) and a grant file's `expires_at` is used verbatim (payer.rs:173-184 parses only the *default* path, when the field is absent). Equal instants written differently therefore get opposite verdicts, and any text that sorts after the clock never expires. The lower-trust principal is whoever supplies the grant JSON to `zanary-probe payer --grant` (architecture.md boundary 3: caller-supplied JSON and paths into the probe CLI). No attacker is even needed: an operator or generic tool that writes the expiry from local time (a legal RFC3339 offset) or with a typo silently widens the authority window, and the control that should have caught it is the grant's own expiry rule ('the instant after which the authority is void', docs/BOUNDED-PAYER.md:31). The failure is invisible after the fact: PayerDecision records no decision time (observation/src/lib.rs:202-214) and payer-policy has no expiry rule (payer_policy.rs:114 only echoes the expiry; a paid row under a grant that expired in 2020 returns Pass).
root_cause: Text comparison of two RFC3339 strings instead of an instant comparison, plus no validation or canonicalisation of `expires_at` on the grant-file path. `if now >= grant.expires_at.as_str()` (payer.rs:91) is only correct when both strings are the same encoding — canonical UTC 'Z', whole seconds, fixed width. The clock producer and the grant author are different components with different conventions: record.rs:132 formats fractional seconds (data/runs/payer-pass/report.json: verified_at "2026-10-16T10:57:34.300715717Z"), data/grants/*.json and the fixtures are whole-second Z, and RFC3339 permits UTC offsets that the comparison misorders ('.' < 'Z', '0' < '1').
intended_behavior: An invoice shown at or after the grant's expiry instant must be refused ('expiry — the instant after which the authority is void', docs/BOUNDED-PAYER.md:31; 'now >= expires_at? -> refuse (authority expired)', docs/BOUNDED-PAYER.md:43), and that refusal must hold for any valid RFC3339 representation of that instant; a value that is not a usable instant should refuse the run rather than read as unexpired.

title: Payments are recorded only after all of them are broadcast: an aborted or repeated run leaves on-chain payments with no ledger and re-pays them
description: The payer decides every invoice first and keeps every decision in memory (payer.rs:244-270), then pays the allowed ones in a loop that propagates every step with `?` (291-363): Address::decode (298), MemoBytes::from_bytes (304), propose (306-307), build+broadcast (308), mine_and_resync (309, 11 blocks, ops::CONFIRM_BLOCKS). ledger.jsonl is the only ledger persistence and, with run.json/findings.json/report.json, is written once, after the loop (409; 411 -> record.rs:45/50/61) with unconditional truncating std::fs::write. A run that dies inside the loop - decide admits an invoice the loop cannot pay (a receiver that does not decode under an allowlist containing that literal, or a memo over the ZIP-302 cap; both re-verified ALLOW offline and the payer's own intake accepts the JSON), an indexer failure, a timeout, or SIGINT - exits with no artifact at all, while any earlier iteration's payment is already broadcast and mined. Nothing outside those artifacts remembers a paid invoice (PayerRun is label+grant+decisions, observation/src/lib.rs:222-230; spent_zat derives from the in-memory decisions, 234-240; no file under crates/ reads a ledger), so re-running the same command re-decides from spent=0 and broadcasts the same payments again; and a completed re-run into the same --out (default data/runs/payer, payer.rs:151-153) replaces the earlier ledger/run/report wholesale. The grant budget is a per-run bound, not a lifetime one, and no source-visible control dedupes invoices or bounds re-execution (companion RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION rules: input = caller-supplied invoice JSON directory; amplification = up to budget_zat re-paid per completed re-run plus the payments of every aborted run; retained state = none, which is the defect itself; recovery = manual reconciliation against the chain; the failure is process-fatal with no supervisor). Calibration: the flow runner commits through the same end-of-run record::write_run_artifacts (flow.rs:502), but the re-pay consequence is the payer's. Same source-derived root cause as sibling candidate `crates/probe/src/payer.rs:payment-loop-failure-aborts-before-ledger-and-run-artifacts-are-written` (hunter-broadcast, wave 2); the two records should be deduped/merged. This record consolidates two fingerprints that independent verification found to share one root cause: this one and `crates/probe/src/payer.rs:payment-loop-failure-aborts-before-ledger-and-run-artifacts-are-written` (filed in wave 2 by hunter-broadcast and independently verified by verifier-1). Its facets are folded in here rather than counted twice: the decide-everything-then-pay ordering, the `?` abort after earlier invoices were already broadcast, the missing `error:` refusal reason the payer-policy property looks for, and the re-pay on re-run.
claimed_root_cause: The spend record is an end-of-run artifact rather than a durable append-only journal written before each broadcast: decisions and refusal lines are buffered in memory (payer.rs:291-379), every payment step returns early through `?` with the chain effect already committed (298-310), the only persistence is after the loop (409, 411) via unconditional truncating std::fs::write, nothing persists a paid-invoice set for the next run to consult (PayerRun = label + grant + decisions), and a reused --out erases the previous evidence. This is the same source-derived root cause as the sibling candidate `crates/probe/src/payer.rs:payment-loop-failure-aborts-before-ledger-and-run-artifacts-are-written` (hunter-broadcast, wave 2): both are the end-of-loop commit plus `?` abort ordering at payer.rs:291-411; the no-persisted-paid-state and overwrite facets here are consequences of the same single end-of-run write design, not a genuinely different defect - dedupe/merge the two records. The same ordering defect was filed independently as `crates/probe/src/payer.rs:payment-loop-failure-aborts-before-ledger-and-run-artifacts-are-written`: one end-of-loop commit plus `?` abort at payer.rs:291-411, reported once here.

description: The publish job republishes each gate run's test.json into public/claims/<artifact>/ (privacy-gate.yml:161, served by upload-pages-artifact at 209-211 and deploy-pages at 213-215) and the same file is uploaded as the gate job's 30-day artifact (privacy-gate.yml:95-104, world-downloadable on this public repository). title: The rig that produces and re-verifies every published privacy claim runs from two mutable :latest image tags
description: Both rig containers are selected by floating tags (harness/docker-compose.yml:9 electriccoinco/zcashd:latest, :34 electriccoinco/lightwalletd:latest). Nothing in the reviewed revision pins a digest, sets pull_policy or platform, or checks a repo digest (git grep '@sha256:' / 'pull_policy' / 'repoDigests' over the tracked tree: 0 hits each; '@sha256:' 0 hits across every commit), so the content that runs is chosen by whoever can re-point those Docker Hub tags, not by this repository. That content is not marginal: zcashd is the chain and the miner, and lightwalletd is the CompactTxStreamer the wallets sync against, so the pair produces every block, transaction and balance the flow runner observes, the gate's chain verification re-reads against the same endpoints (crates/probe/src/gate.rs:165, verify at :156), and the anchor timestamp is a shielded memo on that chain. The resolution point is reached by (a) any third-party workflow that uses the composite action (action.yml:85 runs harness/up.sh on the caller's runner; the action is documented as uses: memeshee/zanary@main), (b) this repo's own gate and payer jobs (.github/workflows/privacy-gate.yml:87 via uses: ./ and :239 directly) including the weekly cron (:23) on runners with no image cache, and (c) the judge-facing one command (README.md:111/114, docs/SUBMISSION.md:36). A substituted image therefore both executes on those machines and can fabricate the data a 'privacy claim' is made of, while the recorded claim carries no image, digest or container identity at all (crates/report/src/lib.rs:33-54 binds version/flow_id/flow_commit/chain/heights/findings/evidence/report_hash only), and the strongest source-visible chain control is a string equality between the node's self-reported getblockchaininfo.chain and the report's own self-asserted 'regtest' (crates/report/src/verify.rs:697) - so a drift is invisible in the evidence, the artifacts and the published page. The docs assert fixed identities that no mechanism enforces (harness/HARNESS.md:54-55 and README.md:75 name v6.20.0 / v0.5.5 next to the mutable tags). Whether the tags have in fact been re-pointed, and who can re-point them, is a registry fact this run cannot observe - hence needs_validation rather than confirmed.
claimed_root_cause: harness/docker-compose.yml selects both rig services by mutable tag (:9, :34) and the repository never binds the running container to a reviewed artifact: no image digest, no pull_policy, no platform pin, no repo-digest comparison anywhere in the tracked tree or history (git grep '@sha256:' / 'pull_policy' / 'repoDigests': 0 hits; the only docker inspect in the tree is harness/up.sh:116 reading .State.Running; the only docker pull is scripts/phase0-warmup.sh:31, recording no digest). The one step that could record what resolved - the bare `docker compose up -d` at harness/up.sh:60 (default pull policy `missing`, so any machine without the image cached pulls it) - records nothing, and the claim schema (crates/report/src/lib.rs:33-54) has no field for it, so the gate verdict and the published evidence are produced by an unbound third-party component.

trace.description: The chain/miner container and the indexer container are selected by floating tags (electriccoinco/zcashd:latest, electriccoinco/lightwalletd:latest); the file pins no digest, platform or pull policy, so the satisfying artifact is decided outside this repository.

`docker compose up -d` resolves those tags on whichever machine runs the harness - compose's default pull policy is `missing`, so a machine with no cached image (a fresh CI runner, a judge) pulls from the registry - and the script records nothing about what it resolved; its only identity-adjacent call (:116) reads .State.Running.

trace.scope: composite action step 'start the throwaway chain'
trace.description: A third-party workflow that consumes `uses: memeshee/zanary@main` executes this step, so the current content of both tags is pulled and run inside the caller's runner/job, which is the execution boundary the tag controller reaches.

This repository's own gate and payer jobs run the same harness/up.sh - the schedule (:23, cron 17 4 * * 1) re-runs it weekly on fresh runners - and the publish job (:110-163) renders the resulting runs to Pages, so the artifact published as the project's public privacy evidence is decided downstream of the unpinned containers.

What a claim binds: version, flow_id, flow_commit, chain ('regtest' as a self-asserted string), verified_at_height, verified_at, ttl_seconds, findings, evidence, merchant_is_simulated, report_hash - no image, digest, container or environment identity, so the container content behind a claim is unrecorded and uncheckable after the fact.

trace.scope: gate verdict (chain_verified) and its published summary
trace.description: The pass/fail verdict is re-derived from the same unbound node+indexer pair (verify_report at :156 reads the live node and indexer; the strongest chain check is the self-reported string at verify.rs:697), and the anchor it may publish (:181-206) is a shielded memo on the chain those containers produce, so the value that reaches the build result, the uploaded artifacts and the public claim index is produced by a component whose identity this repository never fixed or recorded.

evidence.description: image: electriccoinco/zcashd:latest - floating tag, no @sha256 digest, no pull_policy, no platform
image: electriccoinco/lightwalletd:latest - same for the indexer; the second service mounts nothing and adds no identity requirement
the only resolution point: bare `docker compose up -d` (the compose header documents the same command for the user)

run: harness/up.sh in the payer job; the gate job reaches the same step through uses: ./ at :87

documents `electriccoinco/zcashd:latest` (v6.20.0) - a fixed version asserted next to a mutable tag, with no mechanism enforcing either the version or the identity
'zcashd v6.20.0 regtest + lightwalletd v0.5.5, one `docker compose up -d`' - the reproducibility the README sells is not bound to the pulled artifact
'One command: harness/up.sh && scripts/demo-run.sh' - the judge-facing instruction resolves the unpinned tags on the judge's machine
'the run has a timestamp nobody had to be trusted for' - on this rig the timestamp (an anchor memo) and the run share the unpinned containers as their producer
Report struct: the published claim carries no container/image/digest identity, so drift between what produced it and what the docs name is undetectable from the evidence
the strongest source-visible chain control: equality of the node's self-reported getblockchaininfo.chain with the report's own 'regtest' string - a substituted node answers it trivially
even the repo's own warm-up pulls the same floating tag (`electriccoinco/zcashd:latest`) with a bare docker pull, recording no digest

blockers: Registry fact, not observable from source and out of bounds for this run (no registry access, no pull or inspect of the rig's images): which manifest digest docker.io/electriccoinco/zcashd:latest and docker.io/electriccoinco/lightwalletd:latest resolve to, and whether either tag has been re-pointed since the reviewed revision (introduced with the tags in e79f4e6, 2026-10-11; `git log -S':latest' -- harness/docker-compose.yml` returns only that commit).

Consumer fact: whether any run (this repo's weekly cron, a push, or a third-party workflow using the action) executed between the reviewed commit and now against container content that differs from the reviewed-era image; decidable only from the registry plus Actions logs and artifact digests that are outside this unit's reach.

No bounded local check can settle it: the decisive experiment needs a substituted node/indexer pair (a hostile lightwalletd answering CompactTxStreamer plus a node answering JSON-RPC) reachable by the probe, i.e. the rig's own images and host ports (18232/18233/9067/9068) - both explicitly out of bounds - and the approved sandbox (--network=none, no image pulls) cannot build or run them.

validation_plan.local: On a machine allowed to reach the registry (read-only; nothing pushed or published): (1) at two times at least a day apart, resolve both tags without pulling - `docker buildx imagetools inspect electriccoinco/zcashd:latest` and the same for lightwalletd:latest (fallback `docker manifest inspect --verbose <tag>`) - recording the per-platform manifest digest; (2) in a disposable checkout of the reviewed commit run `harness/up.sh` once and immediately capture `docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' zanary-zcashd` and the same for zanary-lwd; a digest that changes between the two observations while harness/docker-compose.yml is unchanged is the missing drift observation, and if the machine that produced the recorded/golden evidence still holds those images, `docker image inspect --format '{{.RepoDigests}}'` it and compare (the recorded evidence itself cannot supply the baseline - that is the finding). Closure (repo-side, non-destructive): pin both services to the observed digests, have harness/up.sh compare the running containers' RepoDigests against the pins before the flow runs, and record the observed digest in the claim/summary so a claim names the container content that produced it.

title: Rig control plane (zcashd JSON-RPC) and the credential-less lightwalletd indexer are published without a host-IP qualifier, so the documented setup inherits the Docker engine's every-interface default, gated only by RPC credentials the public repository itself carries
description: harness/docker-compose.yml publishes the regtest node's JSON-RPC (host port 18232), its unused P2P port (18233) and lightwalletd's gRPC/HTTP (9067/9068) as unqualified PORT:PORT specs; no host interface is named anywhere in that file (mechanically re-derived: 4 publish specs, 0 host-IP-qualified, no loopback qualifier, no host_ip key), so the host-side binding falls to the Docker engine's default for an unqualified publish - every interface on a standard daemon - to be confirmed or refuted on the operator's engine. Nothing on the node then restricts who may authenticate: harness/zcash.conf - seeded verbatim onto a fresh checkout by harness/up.sh - sets rpcbind=0.0.0.0 and rpcallowip=0.0.0.0/0, and the accepted credential is the fixed regtest pair the same repository publishes (compose command line, conf seed, probe client default; equality re-derived by comparison, values never printed). A peer that can reach the port and has read the public repository is therefore the node operator: mine blocks at will (generate), stop the node, read node-wallet state, and invoke file-writing wallet RPCs whose outputs land in the datadir bind-mounted from the host checkout. lightwalletd is started --no-tls-very-insecure on 0.0.0.0 with no credential at all, giving the same peer a channel to the chain. The project's own model assumes the opposite (docs/THREAT-MODEL.md:113 'the harness runs everything on localhost'; harness/HARNESS.md:3 'no network beyond this machine'; HARNESS.md:55 'never expose it' for the no-TLS indexer), while README.md:111-114, docs/CI.md:66 and the composite action (action.yml:85) direct any reader to create the binding, including inside third-party CI jobs on infrastructure the authors do not control. Impact is bounded by the target: regtest only, no real value, no mainnet key material, and the only host path a rig container can write is data/zcashd (docker-compose.yml:18) - which is why this stays a validation lead rather than a confirmed finding: the decisive remaining facts are the engine's effective binding and off-host reachability (host firewall and network), both unobserved here.
claimed_root_cause: The documented one-command local rig publishes its control-plane and indexer ports without a loopback (host-IP) qualifier, and the node is configured to accept RPC from any source (rpcbind=0.0.0.0 / rpcallowip=0.0.0.0/0) under a credential committed to the public repository; no in-repo consumer needs off-host reachability, so the all-interface default binding is an unintended network exposure created wherever the documented setup runs.

title: flow definition jitter_blocks has no upper bound: one accepted line names a mining request of up to 4,294,967,295 blocks, drawn per payment and sent as a single uncancellable `generate` RPC
description: `jitter_blocks: [min, max]` is accepted for any 1 <= min <= max, so a three-field flow definition can name a mining request of up to u32::MAX blocks (flow.rs:133, 166-176). Every draw is the argument to `ops::mine_and_resync(payer, jitter.next())` (flow.rs:645 per invoice, flow.rs:883 for a batch) and reaches zcashd's `generate` RPC as one call (ops.rs:436 -> node.rs:232); the only client-side bound is the 300 s response-read timeout (node.rs:122-125), which abandons the response and sends nothing that could cancel the work. Re-established independently in the approved sandbox: a serde-accepted definition `{"jitter_blocks":[1,4294967295],"jitter_seed":7}` drew 32 values with mean 1,791,207,489 and maximum 4,085,077,839 blocks in a single call, the first draw alone 1,789,459,390 — so the oversized request is the first payment's, not a tail event (matches the hunter's artifact draw-for-draw). What remains undecided from source or bounded local evidence is entirely node-side: zcashd's `generate` is not part of this repository, so whether it honours a count above the 32-bit signed range, whether it keeps generating after the client's socket closes, and what each block costs in time and disk on the shared host are unknown — and they decide the severity.
claimed_root_cause: Jitter::from_definition (flow.rs:166-176) bounds only the shape of the jitter range (1 <= min <= max; malformed ranges fall back to a fixed 3) and never bounds the work the range can name; the drawn value is passed unscaled to the node's `generate` RPC (ops.rs:436 -> node.rs:232), whose execution is not cancellable from the probe's side (the 300 s client read timeout at node.rs:122-125 abandons the response, not the server-side work; no cancel/shutdown path exists anywhere in the probe).

trace.description: the jitter range arrives as caller-controlled JSON (Option<[u32; 2]>, serde default, no validator); no upper bound is applied at deserialization, and u32::MAX is the largest count a definition can name
`Some([min, max]) if min <= max && min >= 1 => (min, max, None)` accepts the range verbatim (line 167); only malformed ranges are bounded, by the fixed-3 fallback at lines 168-176
`self.rng.gen_range(self.min..=self.max)` yields a count up to 4,294,967,295; recorded in jitter.drawn (line 195) and cast to u64 (line 196), never clamped
`ops::mine_and_resync(payer, jitter.next())` runs after every payment (batch path: one call at flow.rs:883 in settle_batch)
the drawn count becomes the one argument of `node.generate(blocks)` (mine_and_resync, ops.rs:433)

the count is the single parameter of the zcashd `generate` RPC, sent as one raw HTTP request (body at node.rs:80-92); this client's only bound is the 300 s read timeout at node.rs:122-125, which abandons the response without sending any cancellation

evidence.description: the acceptance rule for jitter_blocks: min <= max and min >= 1 — no maximum magnitude, no relationship to chain height or run length; the definition-level validation block (flow.rs:253-297) never inspects the field
per-invoice mining call (batch equivalent flow.rs:883); the draw is the only thing controlling the number of blocks

the 300 s response-read timeout (connect is bounded at 30 s, node.rs:94): on timeout the client errors and closes the request whose server-side work continues by construction; no cancel/shutdown path exists in the probe (grep: the only 'kill' is the payer grant's unrelated --kill-file)

observed locally (verifier-19, approved sandbox, disposable copy restored to HEAD sha afterwards): definition jitter_blocks [1,4294967295] + jitter_seed 7 is accepted and 32 draws give max 4,085,077,839, mean 1,791,207,489, first draw 1,789,459,390 — matching agents/hunter-inputs/artifacts/check-jitter-draw.txt draw-for-draw; raw run: agents/verifier-19/artifacts/check-jitter-independent.txt. Correction to the hunter's arithmetic: the 32-draw mean is 1.79e9, not ~1.9e9. Also: [4294967295,4294967295] is accepted and draws exactly 4,294,967,295; malformed [2,1] falls back to fixed 3

the composite action wraps the gate in `timeout "$GATE_TIMEOUT"` (default 2700 s; 124 -> exit 2 at action.yml:122-124), and the gate reaches this same Jitter path via gate.rs:133 flow::run_recording — it bounds the probe's own exposure but sends nothing to the node, so the mining it asked for is unaffected by killing the probe

blockers: zcashd's `generate` implementation is not part of this repository (harness/docker-compose.yml pins the electriccoinco/zcashd image), so whether it honours a block count above the 32-bit signed range, and whether generation continues after the client's 300 s read timeout closes the socket, cannot be decided from source or from bounded local evidence — and that answer decides whether the effect is a rejected request, a hung RPC, or a host-level drain.

Per-block mining cost and disk growth are runtime facts of the running node: this run's protocol puts the rig's containers and host ports (zanary-zcashd, 18232/18233) out of bounds, the approved sandbox is --network=none with rust:1-slim only, and image pulls are not permitted — so no node can be started or reached to measure them.

The named work is finite (<= 4,294,967,295 blocks per call, one call per payment), so the maximum is bounded in principle; what stays unknown is the node's actual rate and whether that work survives client abandonment, which is what a severity statement would need.

validation_plan.local: Runnable only where a disposable node is allowed (not this run's sandbox, which has no node and no network). Create a NEW throwaway container from the locally pinned zcashd image — never the harness's compose project, no published host ports, its own volume — on a fresh container-internal network, and point ZANARY_NODE_RPC_URL at it from a client on that same network. Then through the target's own code: (a) call NodeRpc::generate with a small count (e.g. 2,000) and confirm one request is emitted and honoured (getblockcount advances by 2,000); (b) start one generate with a count large enough to outlast a forced abort (or SIGKILL the probe process mid-call) and poll getblockcount from inside the node container to see whether height keeps climbing after the client socket closes; (c) record the node volume's size before and after. Bound the whole check to a couple of minutes, never request the drawn ~4.29e9, and delete the container and its volume afterwards.
validation_plan.deployment: The rig owner (not this verifier) repeats (b)/(c) on a DISPOSABLE node built from the harness image to measure per-block time and disk growth for a bounded count, then extrapolates the cost of 4,294,967,295 blocks arithmetically instead of letting the real request run — a giant `generate` against a retained rig volume could fill the disk, so the full draw must never be executed against shared rig state. If the end-to-end path must be shown, run the gate once with a definition jitter_blocks [1, 4294967295] against a throwaway node whose volume is discarded, guarded by the node's disk headroom and the action's 2700 s timeout, and watch getblockcount in a bounded window afterwards.

title: Flow-definition amounts are summed with unchecked u64 arithmetic: a two-invoice definition aborts the dev build and wraps silently in the release build
description: Loading a flow definition validates its shape but never its invoice amounts. The total is computed with `sum::<u64>()` in the run header (flow.rs:336), the same unchecked sum decides the funding shortfall (flow.rs:1182 — the fee term is added with saturating_add at 1183, the sum itself is not), and funding_target sums the amounts again and adds the fee budget with plain `+` (flow.rs:1296-1297), so amounts totalling more than u64::MAX overflow: in a dev build (overflow checks on — the build docs/FLOW-RUNNER-NOTES.md:477 and scripts/agent-pay-loop.sh:20 use for `flow`) the process panics before any wallet or node work; in a release build (no [profile] override exists in any of the 5 workspace manifests; the build the CI, the composite action and the demo scripts use) the same input wraps to a smaller total and the run proceeds on it. The only amount bounds are per-amount Zatoshis::from_u64 checks (ops.rs:912 in propose_shielded_payments, ops.rs:983 in pay --invoice), which run later and reject one too-large amount, never the total. Independently verified from a pristine copy of the reviewed commit: dev exits 101 with `attempt to add with overflow` (backtrace frame flow.rs:336:18); the release build prints `184467440737.09551614 ZEC total` for the two-u64::MAX fixture and continues to the node step.
root_cause: No load-time bound on invoice amounts plus unchecked additive arithmetic over definition-controlled u64 values: `invoices.iter().map(|i| i.amount_zat).sum::<u64>()` (flow.rs:336, 1182) and `sum::<u64>() + fee_budget_zat(...)` (flow.rs:1296-1297). The same function guards its fee term with saturating_add (flow.rs:1183), so the unchecked sum and add are outliers inside the code that computes them.
intended_behavior: A definition whose amounts are not payable is refused at load time with a diagnostic naming the invoice — the same place and style as the neighbouring checks — and the arithmetic that consumes amounts cannot overflow for any accepted definition.

trace.description: the --definition file is read and deserialized into FlowDefinition; every amount is caller-controlled (InvoiceSpec.amount_zat: u64 at flow.rs:62, no serde bound and no custom deserializer)
the validation block (lines 253-297) checks the invoice list, receiver_strategy, receipt_account vs merchant_account and settlement/batch uniqueness — amounts are never looked at

`.map(|i| i.amount_zat).sum::<u64>() as i128` overflows: reproduced panic `attempt to add with overflow` (exit 101) with the backtrace frame `run_recording` at flow.rs:336:18, before any wallet or node work
the same unchecked sum decides whether the payer covers the invoices (the fee term is added with saturating_add at 1183; the sum is not)
`sum::<u64>()` (1296) `+ fee_budget_zat(...)` (1297) adds to the already-wrapped total without saturating; its result is the top-up target the run acts on (consumed at flow.rs:424)

evidence.description: the sum that panics in a dev build for two u64::MAX amounts — independently reproduced: exit 101, `attempt to add with overflow`, backtrace frame at ./crates/probe/src/flow.rs:336:18, before NodeRpc::from_env()
sibling control in the same file: `needed.saturating_add(fee_budget_zat(...))` — the author bounded the fee term deliberately, but not the invoice sum it is added to
funding_target (lines 1291-1298) sums the same amounts (1296) and adds the fee budget with plain `+` (1297); the result is the payer top-up target (used at flow.rs:424)

the amount bound, per payment later: Zatoshis::from_u64(*zats) inside propose_shielded_payments rejects one amount above MAX_MONEY; the sibling site ops.rs:983 (`pay --invoice`) is the same per-amount shape — neither bounds a total

no [profile.dev]/[profile.release] section in the workspace or any of the 5 manifests (checked); release builds therefore wrap. CI/action/demo build --release (action.yml:80, .github/workflows/privacy-gate.yml:135/236); verified by building and running both profiles from the reviewed commit
the documented way to run a definition is `./target/debug/zanary-probe flow --definition ...` — the profile in which the overflow panics

conditions.description: a definition whose invoice amounts total more than u64::MAX: two u64::MAX amounts in a 144-byte file (the verified fixture), or — with every amount individually within the consensus money range — at least 8,785 invoices at MAX_MONEY (2,100,000,000,000,000 zatoshis), a few hundred KB of JSON

dev profile (overflow checks on — the build the local docs and scripts use) panics with exit 101; release profile (the CI/action/demo build) wraps silently and the run proceeds on the wrong total. Both observed from binaries built off the reviewed commit: dev exit 101 panic; release printed `184467440737.09551614 ZEC total` for the two-u64::MAX fixture and continued to the node step

execution.attacker_perspective: The flow definition is the untrusted file this CLI takes (caller- or CI-supplied JSON). A definition of a hundred-odd bytes (or a careless one carrying absurd amounts) crashes the dev-build runner where it should have said which invoice is not payable, and in the release build it makes the runner act on a total that is not the sum of the amounts it was given.
payloads: {"flow_id":"hostile-sum","invoices":[{"invoice_id":"1","amount_zat":18446744073709551615},{"invoice_id":"2","amount_zat":18446744073709551615}]} (evil-sum.json, 144 bytes, sha256 6bf0d8114fbb4420359bc81dc498e7a5006ef469f1ec84e91a003e7fded89b5b)
flow --definition evil-sum.json
instructions: In an OS-enforced sandbox with no network, build the reviewed commit from a pristine `git archive HEAD` copy with rust-toolchain.toml removed: `cargo build --offline -p zanary-probe --bin zanary-probe` and `cargo build --offline --release -p zanary-probe --bin zanary-probe` (rustc 1.99.0).

Write the payload JSON to evil-sum.json and run `./target/debug/zanary-probe flow --definition evil-sum.json`; read the exit code and the header output. The run reaches neither the node nor the indexer, so no rig state is touched.

Raw-sum contrast with the same toolchain: `rustc v20-wrap.rs` over `let v = std::hint::black_box([u64::MAX, u64::MAX]); let total: u64 = v.iter().copied().sum::<u64>();` panics with overflow checks on, and `rustc -O v20-wrap.rs` prints 18446744073709551614 without panicking.
Run the release binary on the same fixture: `./target/release/zanary-probe flow --definition evil-sum.json` — the header shows the wrapped total and the run proceeds to the node step.
execution.observed_result: Dev build: exit 101; stdout shows the run header (flow id hostile-sum, flow commit 51b8f57faad49badfeb9a0c963fc86b6229ceed6910a74ee08f12e529b23f02c — identical to the hunter's recorded value, plus settlement/chain lines) and then stderr `thread 'main' panicked at .../library/core/src/iter/traits/accum.rs:206:1: attempt to add with overflow`; with RUST_BACKTRACE=1 the frame is `zanary_probe::flow::run_recording` at ./crates/probe/src/flow.rs:336:18 <- flow::run (flow.rs:230:38) <- main (main.rs:46:41) — the panic is raised evaluating the header sum at flow.rs:336, before NodeRpc::from_env(). Release build of the same source: no panic; the header prints `invoices : 2 (184467440737.09551614 ZEC total)` (the wrapped 2^64-2 total; the true total would be 368934881474.19103230 ZEC) and the run continues to the node step (exit 1 there with `Connection refused`, since the sandbox has no node) instead of rejecting the definition. A benign control (two 100,000-zat invoices) prints 0.00200000 ZEC total and reaches the same node step in both builds. The optimised raw-sum snippet printed 18446744073709551614 (exit 0); the unoptimised one panicked identically. Transcripts: agents/verifier-20/artifacts/check-panics-repro.txt, agents/verifier-20/artifacts/check-release-binary.txt, agents/verifier-20/artifacts/check-release-wrap.txt.

remediation.strategy: Validate amounts where the definition is loaded (each within the consensus money range, and the total via checked_add) and make every later sum checked or saturating, so an unpayable definition is a diagnostic instead of a panic or a wrapped number.

likelihood.reason: The overflow needs amounts totalling above u64::MAX; a 144-byte two-invoice file is enough to reach it, but no realistic definition gets there by accident and the file is the caller's own. The release-mode wrap is reachable with individually-plausible amounts only through 8,785+ invoices at MAX_MONEY.

impact.reason: Dev build: the run aborts before any wallet or node work (exit 101, no diagnostic naming the invoice). Release build: the run proceeds on a wrapped total and fails later on its own per-amount checks (ops.rs:912/983 reject amounts above MAX_MONEY) or an unrelated node error. No funds, keys or authority are exposed — the wallet involved is the operator's own throwaway regtest wallet.

confidence.reason: Both halves were reproduced independently in the network-off sandbox from a pristine copy of commit 7058406 (all tracked files verified byte-identical to the read-only target): the dev binary exits 101 with the panic backtrace frame at flow.rs:336:18, and the release binary of the same source prints the wrapped total for two u64::MAX amounts and continues instead of rejecting the definition. The unchecked sites and the saturating sibling control are visible in the reviewed source. Nothing stronger than the claim was observed — the downstream funding-target consequence stays source-established because it needs a live node.
